rv.q: The evening proves an Anglo-American triumph.
As bio-musicals go, this is as good as it gets.
This show is a great deal better than most jukebox musicals.
Even folk who are inclined to be sniffy about jukebox musicals will be overwhelmed by this one.
But in the end, wrapped around the bare bones of this extraordinary woman’s life, we watch a Tina Turner tribute band of supreme quality.
As big, noisy, uncomplicated musicals go, it’s a lot of fun.
Warren does not mimic Turner: she captures her voice and releases it. She is the fire in a show that could do with more flare.
But too often Phyllida Lloyd’s production struggles to make a sensitive synthesis of the two.
This musical never fully sparks into life...Simply the best? Not quite.
Here, alas, there’s no nuance at all.

Hooray! I have a new favourite West End show and I urge you to see it for a fantastic night of musicality, drama and lots and lots of Tina Turner. Centre Adrienne Warren (Tina Turner) and the cast of Tina. Photo by Manuel Harlan.
Warren's knockdown performance here not only elevates an otherwise routine bio-musical into a triumph, it's a slam-dunk for every upcoming awards ceremony.
It's everything you expected, executed well and packs in a few surprises.

This is a unique jukebox musical that isn't scared to delve into difficult themes including racism and spousal abuse to highlight Turner's tough journey to stardom and her extraordinary courage and drive to succeed.
Tina: The Tina Turner Musical is an ambitious musical tackling more than you might expect from a show of this genre.
It’s good to have the show back.

Tina is mostly a high-voltage showcase for Warren, who is rarely offstage and constantly in motion for almost the entirety of this two-hours-plus production. Petite and slender, the 31-year-old Virginia native lacks Turner's warrior-queen physique and earthy, sweat-soaked, thunderdome roar.
The problem for me is that, at least for the first act which charts her relationship with Ike, what we actually witness is a strong woman being brought down by multiple acts of violence.
Phyllida Lloyd's dazzling production has you in its grip throughout.

Apart from a sharp focus on her physical abuse at the hands of her first husband, Ike (a bravely brutal Kobna Holdbrook-Smith), Turner’s emotional problems are glossed over. The treatment of her family relationships is so confused that I presumed she was adopted.
